newsitem.title: UK: Irish minister allays fears of new IRA violence.
newsitem.headline: Irish minister allays fears of new IRA violence.

text.p: Soothing remarks by Ireland's deputy prime minister Dick Spring appeared on Wednesday to have allayed fears in Northern Ireland of a new outbreak of Irish Republican Army (IRA) violence.

Renewed concern arose on Tuesday after British Prime Minister John Major effectively rejected proposals for a new IRA ceasefire put to him by the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein and moderate Catholic leader John Hume.
After a 17-month ceasefire the IRA renewed its military campaign against British rule in Northern Ireland last February but has not carried out any attacks for nearly two months.
This has prompted speculation that it has been operating an unofficial truce in the hope of getting Sinn Fein into talks on the future of Northern Irleland.
But Major said on Tuesday that Britain was not prepared to alter its policy on Northern Ireland.
Spring said he did not believe Major's response was a final or completely negative one. Negotiations for a new ceasefire would continue, he said.
"We are going to continue with our efforts to bridge the gap that exists. The prize is worth taking risks for, and I believe everybody interested in the process will do so," Spring said.

Under the Hume-Sinn Fein proposals, Sinn Fein would be admitted to the talks chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell as soon as the IRA renewed its ceasefire. Demands that the guerrillas disarm immediately would be dropped and a strict timetable would be set for the talks.
They also called for goodwill proposals from Britain, such as the release of some IRA prisoners.
Sinn Fein has been barred from the talks until the IRA abandons violence and gives up its arms.
The party's leader, Gerry Adams, said Major's rejection of the plan meant the IRA would not call a new truce, raising fears in Northern Ireland of new guerrilla attacks.
But the Irish Independent said "intense behind-the-scenes negotiations" between republican leaders and the British and Irish governments were "keeping alive the prospect of a new IRA ceasefire."
"Ceasefire hopes survive Major rebuff," said the front page headline in the Dublin-based newspaper.

Major's rejection early this year of a proposal by Mitchell that the disposal of arms should be addressed during the talks provoked the IRA into abandoning its ceasefire and setting off the first of a series of attacks on British targets.
The republicans' rivals, pro-British "Loyalists", have been allowed into the peace talks because their guerrillas are still honouring a ceasefire originally called to match the IRA's.
Hume has accused Major of rejecting his plan for a new IRA truce to satisfy unionist politicians in the British parliament on whom Major relies to shore up his majority of just one.
Unionists, who can usually be relied on to vote with the government, have threatened to withdraw their support if Major makes any concessions to the republicans.
